questions.q: Put the steps of a linear search in order.
steps: Start at the first item in the list
Compare the item with the one being searched for
If it does not match, move to the next item
Stop when it is found or the end of the list is reached
questions.feedback: Start, compare, move on, stop. There is nothing cleverer to it, which is both its weakness and its strength.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.1 Lesson 6 — Search corridor, station 1: How it works

questions.q: A linear search looks for the value 19 in the list [4, 8, 11, 15, 19, 23, 42]. How many comparisons does it make?
questions.feedback: It checks 4, 8, 11, 15 and then 19: five comparisons.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.1 Lesson 6 — Search corridor, station 1: How it works

questions.q: In the worst case, how many comparisons does a linear search of a list of 40 items make?
questions.feedback: The worst case is the item being last, or not there at all, so every item is checked.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.1 Lesson 6 — Search corridor, station 1: How it works

questions.example: A linear search works on a list in any order, while a binary search needs a sorted one, so a linear search can be used straight away without paying the cost of sorting the list first.
questions.paraphrase: It does not require the data to be sorted, which means it can be run immediately on an unordered list rather than sorting it beforehand.
questions.feedback: No ordering needed, and then why that is worth something.
